Reading This as a Brief

What follows previews the whole system before you've built any of it — on purpose — and what to do with names you don't recognize yet.

The rest of this lesson previews the entire system: every entity, the full technology stack, and the reasoning behind the biggest structural decisions — including several you haven't learned the mechanics of yet, like background job queues and event-driven notifications. That breaks the normal rule for every lesson after this one, where new material only ever builds on what's already been covered. This lesson is the deliberate exception, for the reason the previous page laid out: a brief exists to describe the whole shape of a system up front, not to teach it piece by piece.

So when a term below doesn't fully land yet, that's expected, not a sign you're missing something you should already know. Treat it the way you'd skim a project's README before touching its code: you're building a rough map of what exists and roughly why, not mastering any one piece of it. Every concept named here gets its full, hands-on treatment in the lesson that actually introduces it — this page will get referenced back from there, so the two connect once you've seen both sides.

Two things worth watching for as you read:

  • What's fixed vs. what's a starting point. The domain model (next topic) is the shape of the data for the whole course — it doesn't change. Individual technology choices (this lesson's third topic) are presented with their reasoning, not as facts to memorize, because the reasoning is the transferable part. A different project, a different constraint, and the same reasoning could land on a different choice.
  • Why, not just what. Anywhere this brief says a decision was made "so that" something else is true, that's the part worth holding onto. It's the same habit that matters when directing an agent yourself one day: stating the why behind a request is what lets an agent make good judgment calls on the parts you didn't spell out, instead of guessing blind.
